subject: vikingFeast
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: Viking longhouse feast table.
Style: Valheim.
reasoning:
I need to build this as a static prop model rather than a rigged creature, aiming for a rich part count in the 180-340 range with 5-12 textures to capture the Viking longhouse feast table aesthetic. I'm planning to keep the geometry in model space under the root, defining parts with their geometry and color data.

For the design, I'm laying out a long trestle table roughly 3.2m long along X, 0.9m wide, 0.78m tall, with thick planked top, carved end boards, and benches on both front and back long sides facing +Z. I'll populate it with wooden trenchers, drinking horns and tankards, a roast boar centerpiece, bread loaves, a cheese wheel, apples, iron candelabra for lighting, an embroidered knotwork table runner, and possibly a mead barrel at one end to round out the feast setting.

Now I'm planning the Valheim-style detailing: rough dark wood, iron bands, leather lashing, hewn planks, carved knots, rune textures, and dragon-head carvings on the end posts, with the boar as the hero prop and other food items (fish, chicken, mugs, bread basket) filling out the spread, plus glowing candle flames to light the scene.

I'm defining coordinates for the table geometry, setting the length along X from -1.6 to 1.6, width with half-extent 0.475 along Z, and building the tabletop from five planks each about 0.19 wide and 0.06 thick with small gaps and grain texture variation along the X axis to give a weathered wood-plank look.

Now I'm working out the underframe trestles at the table ends, trying to shape an arched, dragon-leg-like cutout profile using an extruded 2D outline, but finding concave polygon outlines risky to get right, so I'm simplifying to splayed leg boxes combined with a separate extruded foot block instead of one complex concave shape.

I'll also add foot runner beams flat on the floor at each end, and maybe carve dragon-head details at their tips for a Viking touch.

Now I'm plotting the outline points for a carved end board with a gothic arch cutout, defining the coordinates to shape the curve symmetrically.

Still tracing outline points...

Confirming winding is CCW and non-self-intersecting, so I'll skip smoothing and use a small bevel instead. Then I'm working out the board placement and thickness so the top plank surface lines up at 0.80, positioning side boards at x=±1.15 with proper axis orientation.

For decoration, I'm planning a flat decal plane glued just off each board's outer face (±0.038 offset for 0.07 thick boards), textured with an engraved-looking knotwork or Valknut pattern in dark brown with transparent background, oriented to face outward along ±x.

Then for structure, I'm placing a stretcher beam running along x at y≈0.60, about 0.09 tall and 0.12 thick, roughly 2.9 long so it protrudes slightly past the end boards (~0.15 each side), with small tapered wedge boxes at the ends standing in as locking keys, typical of Viking trestle table construction.

For the tabletop, I'm making it 3.2 long so it overhangs the end boards (at ±1.15) by 0.45 on each side, and adding cross cleats under the planks atop the boards. I need to adjust the board height to around 0.70 so the cleats and plank bottoms don't awkwardly intersect the boards.

Now I'm moving to the benches: placed along the front and back at z=±0.80, 2.8 long, seat at 0.46 height with 0.06 thickness and 0.26 width, with slab legs at x=±1.0 that I'll shape using a simple extruded trapezoid outline rather than a complex notched profile.

I'm shaping the bench end-boards with an arched extrude profile spanning the seat width, legs positioned at x=±1.05, and considering adding a sheep-fur throw on one bench for texture.

I'll add a folded striped wool blanket as a painted box for color, plus a flattened mottled-sphere fur pelt, keeping extras moderate. For the head of the table, I'm thinking of including a carved high-back chair at x≈1.95 facing inward with finial posts and a decorated back panel, weighing whether it fits the overall 3.2-unit table width.

Actually I'll keep it simple: a basic chair with seat, back, posts topped with horse-head finials (cone plus sphere) and armrests. For the tabletop, I'm working out a thin runner cloth across the surface, deciding between a textured box or a flat plane oriented so its top face displays the decal properly.

Since the pattern is symmetric along both axes, the exact orientation handedness doesn't matter. The texture itself is a red cloth with gold trim featuring a repeated Valknut/knot border pattern, sized at a 2.7:0.42 aspect ratio to match the runner's dimensions on the table.

I'll go with a plane for the runner pattern since the texture reads better than a painted box, maybe adding a thin colored strip underneath for thickness. I'm considering adding fringe tassels at both ends using small hanging cards angled downward near the table edges.

I'm deciding the runner should stay around 3 units long so the fringe lays flat on the table instead of overhanging, and I'll just paint the fringe detail directly into the texture rather than modeling it as geometry. Now I'm laying out the centerpiece items along the table—starting with a roast boar on a large wooden platter at the center, which I'll build as an extruded oval shape for the platter base.

Working out the platter and boar geometry...

Legs are simple tucked capsules, with garnishes of herb sprigs, apples, and cabbage around the boar, plus a skewer and darker paint stripes across the back for crackling texture. I'm positioning the boar centered at x=0 facing +x, then laying out other platters along the x-axis, starting with round bread loaves with cross-scoring on a wooden board at x=-0.95.

Planning the rest of the feast spread: a cheese wheel with a wedge cut and knife at x=-0.5, an iron stew cauldron with ladle at x=0.55, a fish platter with two salmon-like fish on wood at x=0.95, and a bowl of apples and turnips at x=1.35, with an ale barrel possibly going at x=-1.35.

I'm placing a small mead keg with tap right on the table near x=-1.35, lathed with staves and iron bands. Then I'm laying out place settings along both benches — four seats per side with wooden trenchers, horn tankards banded in iron, and knives.

Now I'm adding tankards at the front seats and drinking horns resting in little iron tripod stands on the back side, varying tankard colors, and positioning plates and drinks slightly offset from the table edges so they sit clear of the center runner.

Place settings need to sit outside the runner's half-width, so I'm pushing plate centers further toward the edges while keeping tankards offset from them, then planning candelabra placement flanking the boar platter at the table's center.

Along the central runner I'm laying out items left to right: a keg near the far end, a bread board with loaves, then an iron candelabra, then a cheese wheel positioned so it clears the boar platter's footprint, adjusting x-coordinates to avoid overlap between each piece.

Adjusting candelabra and bread positions slightly to avoid overlap, then checking the boar platter boundary against the cheese edge on the left side. On the right, I'm placing the stew pot, second candelabra, fish platter, and apple bowl with enough spacing to keep them from colliding.

Now I'm setting seat positions along the table at even spacing, keeping plates offset outward so they don't intersect the central runner items like the keg. I'm thinking about adding small scattered details like dice, rune stones, or spilled apples for texture, then working out how to render the candle flames with a glowing cone and sphere combo for the flicker effect.

I'm also planning the surface textures: an embroidered red runner with gold interlace trim, a carved knotwork decal for the end boards in an Urnes-style serpent loop, and a rune-engraved strip along the front edge of the table planks.

For the runes, instead of relying on fonts, I'm sketching each character as simple line-segment strokes within a small grid cell, defining shapes like Fehu's vertical stem with diagonal branches by hand.

Still mapping rune stroke paths...

Let me reconsider the proportions — with a strip that long and thin, I need enough runes to fill it without stretching each glyph too wide, so 56 runes at a cell width of 10 and height of 20 gives a reasonable 28:1 aspect that should render cleanly at a larger canvas size.

Simplifying to a 56-rune band with cell width 20 and height 20, giving a viewBox of 1120x20 at 2048px output — close enough to the 1.14:1 aspect ratio I need, with stroke width scaled to stay crisp at ~3.7px.

Still writing the glyph rune row...

Now I need to confirm the text plane's z-position sits correctly against the front plank surface — checking the five plank z-centers (-0.38 to 0.38, each 0.19 wide) to make sure the engraved band aligns properly with its slight 0.002 offset outward.

For the plate placement, I'm figuring out the y-range (0.745–0.795) for the band spanning plank height 0.05, applying the same logic to both front and back faces with the back using a reversed normal direction. Then I'm sketching out remaining decorative elements to tackle — herb sprigs, painted food textures for bread and fish, carved board textures reused for chair panels, and simple top-down plate/food illustrations for the trenchers.

For the keg details, I'm planning a cradle setup with the barrel lying on its side, axis running along z, lid facing forward with a decal (horn or rune symbol), tap positioned at the front, and building the barrel shape using a lathe geometry.

Since the torus defaults to a z-axis orientation, I can skip the rotation and place the keg directly lying along z, with the head facing front toward +z so the decal reads correctly. I'm sizing it to fit the table runner width and positioning its center height to sit on the cradle, which I'll build from two small wedge supports.

For the cradle itself, I'll use crossbar boxes under the barrel at z=±0.09 plus small 45°-rotated wedge chocks on either side to keep it from rolling. I'm also tallying up the texture/decal needs across the scene: runner, carving board, rune strip, meat and bone plates, herb card, keg head, and possibly bread board, cheese, and engraved horn or tankard emblem decals.

I'm adding fir sprig and sprig-pattern cards as scattered greenery decoration leaning near the candles, bringing the texture count to roughly 8-9 plus base wood paints. Now I'm tallying overall part counts: planks, battens, boards with decals, beam and wedges, bench seats and legs, and per-setting items like lathe-turned plates, food textures, and tankard cylinder-and-band geometry.

I'm also totaling parts for horns, boar, candelabra, keg, bread, cheese, pot, fish, apple bowl, chairs, sprig cards, and blankets/pelt, landing near 250 parts overall. For small details like nail pegs on benches and planks, I'm deciding to skip merging geometries via BufferGeometryUtils to avoid import/path risks, and instead keep them as individual simple cylinder parts since the part budget allows it, while planning materials to stay within the 64 flat-color limit since paints don't count against that.

Defining wood paint helpers using grain and countershade functions to get a weathered dark-oak look with warmer lit tops, with grain axis set to x for planks/benches and y for vertical boards — keeping part counts in check while using the box geometry's UV paint system for each piece.

Writing box/cylinder/sphere helper functions, with rotation handled as degree arrays and scale accepted as vectors, plus a flat option for faceted spheres...

I'll use dir rather than rotation angles for aiming, since it's clearer. Now I'm starting to write the setup module, importing the builder utilities and helper functions I'll need.

Finalizing module imports...

I'm setting up the builder with a name for the feast table and considering a larger paint size for finer detail, since the painted surface area is fairly large at roughly 20 square meters.

Writing wood paint helper...

Adding floor grime darkening near low y-values, then defining several named wood material variants (plank, board, bench) using different color palettes and grain axes.

I also need metal materials for iron, steel, bronze with verdigris, gilt, and copper, plus per-plank grain variation using different seeds. For the plate textures, I'm sketching a food layer using an SVG circle with roast slices and carrots drawn on a transparent background so the wood plate shows through.

Sketching the meat plate SVG with rotated ellipses for the roast slab, a lighter highlight tone, and a pink cut-section, then adding a turnip with cream base and purple top, small green peas, and a golden bread piece before moving to a leftover-bones plate variant.

I'm organizing textures into three groups—meat, bread/cheese/apple, and bones—cycling across three plate variants while keeping the total texture count under budget. Now I'm shaping the plate itself as a shallow trencher using a lathed outline profile.

Still writing plate geometry...

For tankards I'm thinking a tapered cylinder shape for the wooden body, with a stave-like striped texture applied along one axis to mimic barrel construction.

I'm adding iron bands as thin cylinders near the top and bottom rims, then working out a swept-path handle curve positioned outward from the tankard toward the table's edge.

For the ale itself, I'm layering a cream foam disc on top of an amber liquid cylinder below it, then moving on to drinking horns -- tapered ivory sweeps with a radius function that narrows toward the tip, curved along a bezier path and resting in an iron stand.

Writing horn geometry...

I'm plotting the horn's curve from mouth to tip, checking that the tube radius stays below the center height at each point along the path so it doesn't clip through the ground, then setting up a rotation transform for the final placement.

Now I'm working out seat positions around the table, placing plates, tankards, and horns for each side, and checking that horn length and placement don't overlap with the neighboring plate's radius.

I'm reworking the horn placements to avoid colliding with the apple bowl and fish platter, putting horns at the back seats pointed outward and tankards at the front seats, checking each item's x/z offsets against neighboring dishes to confirm clearance.

I'll simplify the horn placement by having each seat's horn point outward from center using its sign, checking clearance against the stew pot and other seat props as I space them out.

For the front setup, I'm positioning tankards, plates, and small knives (blade plus wood handle as boxes) relative to each seat, then starting to think through where to place a bench along the front edge.

Now I'm working out the bench geometry: positioning two benches at z=±0.78 with seat tops at y=0.43, plus end boards with a notched outline at the corners, and adding a pelt and woolen blanket as decorative details on the seats.

For the blanket I'm layering stripe-painted boxes to look folded with a rolled end, placed on the back bench; for the pelt I'm flattening a sphere and giving it a mottled paint texture on the front bench, though I'm wondering if a more detailed tufted sheepskin is too much complexity for this pass.

Now I'm sketching the sheepskin as a mottled flattened sphere with five small flattened lobes around the edges to suggest leg shapes. Then I'm moving on to the chair at the head of the table, positioning its seat, legs, and back with explicit coordinates so it faces toward the table.

Writing chair frame coordinates...

I realize a single chair unbalances the table composition toward +x, so I should mirror it — add a matching chair at the opposite end for a lord-and-lady seating arrangement, symmetric around x=0, perhaps with a different fur color for the second chair.

Now I'm sketching the candelabra: an iron stand with a flared lathe-profile base, a central rod, and three curved arms holding candle cups, rising about 0.35 above the table surface.

Still writing candle and flame details...

Now I'm working out the boar's placement on the platter — stacking the runner, oval platter layers, and figuring the top surface height so the boar's ellipsoid body sits correctly above it.

For the legs, I'm using capsule shapes splayed outward from the body corners down to the platter surface, with small dark trotter spheres at the tips, then starting on the head geometry.

Now I'm detailing the pig's face features: a tapered snout with nostril dots, outward-tilted ear cones, curved cream tusks jutting up from the sides, dark eyes with highlights, and a red apple sphere placed at the mouth.

I'm also planning a curling tail at the back and a row of small bristle cones running along the dorsal ridge, calculating their positions along an arc to follow the pig's back curve.

Since bristles may not suit a roasted presentation, I'm shifting to painting the skin instead -- a glazed orange-brown countershade with darker stripe scoring and char patches via noise, defining the color/paint function for the boar skin texture.

Now I'm planning the garnish layout around the platter: apples as red spheres, flattened cabbage leaves with stripe texture, herb sprig cards oriented with upward-facing frames leaning outward, plus turnip wheels in cream/purple, sizing and positioning each element for a natural scattered presentation.

Moving to the cheese wheel itself, I'm shaping a textured cylinder with color spots, then carving out a wedge cut using a triangular extrusion to suggest a slice removed from the wheel.

For the rind, I'm using a countershading technique based on vertical face normals so the top reads as creamy yellow while the sides darken into a rind color, tuning the level and softness for a believable blend. Then I'm starting on the bread setup with a small wooden board as the base for the loaves.

Still defining the pot profile points...

I'll add the pot's arched handle with rim lugs, a leaning wooden ladle, and set the whole thing on a wooden trivet. Skipping the cauldron legs, I'll move on to designing the fish platter with an oval board and two fish bodies.

For the fish, I'm shaping a flattened sphere for the body with a forked tail plane oriented vertically as if seen from the side, swimming upright, plus a small dorsal fin and eyes, and applying scale and countershade patterns for a silvery look on the back and belly.

Now I'm planning an apple bowl: a lathed wooden bowl with a profile curve, filled with seven apple spheres in red and green tones arranged in a pile with stems, plus a keg lathed along the z-axis with staved paint pattern based on angular position.

For the keg, I'm working out iron hoop placement as torus shapes matching the barrel's radius at different heights, with a circular runic emblem decal on the head for decoration.

I still need a brass tap near the bottom front of the keg, positioning it based on the cradle height and barrel center, then I'll add flat fir sprigs lying on the tabletop as decorative card elements.

For textures I'm settling on nine total: RUNNER, CARVE, RUNES, three FOOD variants, HERB, FIR, and KEG, giving separate leaf-garnish and greenery looks. I'm also weighing whether to add a die, a rune stone, or a chew bone, but deciding to skip the hanging iron nails and focus instead on nailing the Valheim aesthetic—hewn dark timber with warm firelight glow across the surfaces.

I'm working out plank variation details: slightly different lengths and offsets, thickness with small y jitter, tone differences by seed, and placing small wooden peg dowels along the battens at specific x positions for about ten pegs total. I'm deciding to skip bevel trims on the table edges, and considering whether to add dragon or horse-head carvings at the ends of the stretcher beam.

Now I'm sketching a stylized dragon head silhouette for the beam ends, defining the outline as a polygon of points tracing the neck, crest tip, brow, snout, and jaw before closing back to the base, and checking whether this polygon self-intersects.

Positioning the dragon heads at the beam ends, slightly below the beam centerline to match the beam's thickness, so the neck base aligns smoothly with where the beam terminates.

Now I'm working out small gold eye spheres positioned relative to the head's own local coordinate frame, and figuring out the correct thickness axis for the mirrored side using a cross product of the frame's x and y axes.

Picking more palette names, keeping the count under 64 for safety. Now I'm setting up the build function skeleton with a seeded RNG and a helper for placing box geometry parts with color and position.

Writing helper types...

Still writing helper functions...

Now I'm designing the runner SVG texture: a deep red background with a gold inner border trim, and a repeating diamond-knot motif running along the center.

Writing fringe details...

For the end boards I'm sketching a Valknut-style design: three overlapping triangles rotated 120 degrees apart around the center, drawn as stroke-only outlines to form the interlaced knot pattern.

I'll give these carved lines a dark engraved look by layering a light offset highlight stroke behind a thicker dark stroke, plus corner spiral/scroll knotwork and a dashed border ring to frame the design.

Working out the carving region dimensions, I'm adjusting the arch top height and the carving plane coordinates so the engraved square fits properly within the board without overlapping the arch opening.

Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG glyphs...

Now I'm designing the food texture SVGs on a 100x100 viewBox, starting with a meat-and-veg variant that uses rotated ellipses for the roast shape, a lighter inner ellipse for shading, a cut-face path, and small circular garnish accents.

I'm sketching turnip and pea clusters as simple shapes, then adding a small bone sliver for the first plate type. For the other two plate varieties, I'm planning a bread-and-cheese-and-apple combo (triangle wedge cheese with holes, rounded bread slice, circle apple) and a leftovers plate with fish bones, crumbs, and an apple core. Finally I'm assigning these three plate types across the seated characters, mixing them up between front and back rows.

Now I'm working out herb and fir sprig icons: a stem path with rotated leaf ellipses for the herb card, checking stroke widths scale properly at render size, and a zigzag needle pattern built from short paired lines for the fir sprig.

For the keg emblem, I'm designing a circular shield with an outer ring, a stylized drinking horn crescent shape in gold, and a dashed rune border around the circle's edge.

Now I'm setting up the build with imports for the builder toolkit including paint, grain, noise, and shading utilities, plus kits for glow and metal effects, and defining starting constants like the top boundary height for the structure.

I'm defining a wood paint helper that blends top and side grain textures with countershading, then darkens areas using noise-based smoothstep masks for a weathered, grounded look.

Setting up plank geometry and offsets, generating box pieces with varied lengths and wood textures for each plank position...

Centering cleats at 0.72 with planks resting at 0.74, I'm adding small peg cylinders near each cleat-plank intersection, then starting on the end board shape using a polygon outline that traces a decorative scalloped silhouette.

I'm mirroring the end boards across x for symmetry, extruding the same outline with beveled edges, then positioning a carved texture plane on the board face aligned with the upper board region.

Since the board sits at both x positions with thickness extending inward and outward, I need to place carve planes at each face accordingly, looping over both sides to cover the outer and inner surfaces.

For the stretcher, I'm sizing a horizontal box spanning between the boards at a height where it stays within the solid region above the arch, with dragon heads capping both ends and small wedge keys fitted at the joint locations, rotated slightly and painted to match the dark board tone.

I'm also checking the dragon head placement at the beam's outer end -- adjusting its vertical position so the crest doesn't poke through the plank's underside while still overlapping the beam's neck for a clean joint.

I'm placing small gold spheres as eyes at the head's local coordinates, accounting for head thickness so they sit symmetrically on each side, plus adding a nostril detail. Then I'm starting the bench geometry, positioning bench boxes at symmetric z-offsets along the structure.

Now I'm defining the bench end outline as a 2D profile with a notched top for the seat support, extruding it into a thin wedge shape, and planning a lower brace plank connecting the bench ends beneath the seat.

Giving the pelt a mottled cream-brown texture with small leg lobes around the edges, and adding a folded two-layer blanket on the back bench with contrasting striped patterns for variety.

Now I'm defining a plate function that places a lathed wooden base plate at the table surface height with a circular ceramic-textured top, rotated per seat. I need to double-check the vertical offsets so the plate floor and circle surface align properly relative to the table top.

Actually, grain along "y" would streak vertically which looks noisy on a flat top face, so I should switch the plates to grain axis "x" instead.

Now I'm building the tankard function, shaping a tapered cylindrical mug body with iron hoop bands placed near the top and bottom of the cup using their own radii matching the wood taper.

I'm interpolating the hoop radii along the taper so they sit slightly larger than the wood at each height, adding a foam cap cylinder near the top, and now sketching a curved handle using a Catmull-Rom sweep with a few control points on the side of the mug.

Still writing sweep logic...

Shaping the blade as a tapered pentagon outline and extruding it, keeping the geometry cheap with a box handle and pommel.

Working through the cross product, the thickness axis comes out along -y, which centers the blade nicely for a thin sharp extrusion. Now I'm sketching the handle as a short wooden cylinder offset backward from the attachment point, and starting to define a horn function with position, direction sign, and yaw parameters.

I'm plotting the horn's curve path using a cubic bezier from mouth to tip, checking the tube radius tapering and verifying the midpoint height clears the surface properly.

I'm checking horn curvature direction to avoid collisions with the seat plate and neighboring seats, confirming the tip positions stay clear given the 0.67 spacing between seats.

Writing torus geometry for mouth rim...

Still writing candelabra geometry...

Checking the candle height math against the chair top, then moving to the flame glow effect with layered balls for the outer and inner light, plus a wax color and small drip detail. Now I'm setting up the platter as an oval using an ellipse of points.

Setting the runner plane position and placing the boar base at y=0.846, I'm defining an ellipsoid helper using a sphere geometry with non-uniform scale for the body radii, and thinking about whether normals need correction after the scaling for proper shading.

Now I'm positioning the boar's anatomy: the main body ellipsoid, a rear haunch bulge, a shoulder bump, and a slightly lower head ellipsoid, each with specific center coordinates and radii relative to the platter top.

Placing the snout, nostrils, and starting work on the eyes...

I'm calculating where the eyes sit on the head's ellipsoid surface using the surface equation, positioning small dark spheres for closed, roasted-looking eyes, then moving to shape the ears as angled spikes with a base position, direction vector, length, and radius.

Now I'm working out the tusks as smaller cream-colored spikes near the snout, then adding an apple as a red ball resting near the mouth. I'm checking the geometry so the apple actually sits on the platter rather than overhanging it, adjusting the platter's radius outward to fit both the snout and apple comfortably.

Then I'm nudging the whole boar's position slightly left to fit its layout, and recalculating spacing for the neighboring dishes—shifting the cheese further left, moving the candelabra outward, and adjusting the stew pot and fish platter so none of their bases overlap on the table.

I keep running into overlap problems trying to pack the bread board, candle, and cheese wheel tightly together, so I'm reconsidering the layout — maybe shrinking the board, shifting the candle, or moving the cheese off-center onto the bread board itself to avoid collisions.

Let me just recompute positions and half-extents for each item from the keg outward: keg, bread board, candelabra, cheese, boar platter on the left side, then pot, candelabra, and fish trivet mirrored on the right, checking that each pair's edges clear each other.

Now I'm placing small garnish pieces around the boar platter -- a few apples near the rear and sides, keeping them within the rim margin so they don't overlap the boar's body.

For the herb cards, I'm positioning them around the platter edge, leaning outward along the normalized direction from the platter center, and setting up a flow function to drive that orientation per index.

Then I'm moving on to a fish platter design: an oval wooden board holding two fish lying head-to-tail, each modeled as an ellipsoid body positioned above the board surface.

Now I'm working out the fish anatomy details—placing the forked tail as a flat extruded arrow shape extending outward from each fish's rear along its body axis, and starting on the dorsal fin as a small triangular extrusion on top.

Still placing scene elements...

Still defining chair geometry...

Positioning the dragon finial and eyes for symmetry, then laying out the back panel between the posts with a carved texture plane.

I'm sketching a top rail above the back panel and then adding armrests supported by front posts, working out their coordinates relative to the seat height.

For the arms, I'm positioning them with rounded ball ends and connecting the back to the posts. I'm also figuring out the seat cushion as a textured box using fur or leather coloring depending on whether it's for the lord or lady, and considering whether to add a draped pelt over the back rail.

Now I'm defining the chair wood material, adding bronze trim bands around the posts as small boxes, and double-checking the overall chair height works out. I'm also sizing the candelabra and flame heights, and setting up a glow effect on the flame parts since each ball returns a Part with a mesh I can glow.

Then I'm skipping extra lantern and dice details to keep the texture count reasonable, and running a rough part-count estimate across the table setup — planks, pegs, boards, benches, chairs, plates, and tankards — to make sure the overall scene stays manageable.

Continuing the estimate for horns, candelabras, boar, platter, garnish, cheese, bread, pot, fish, apples, keg, and runner, landing around 330 total parts with low triangle counts, which feels reasonable. Now I'm starting to write the actual build function, defining a seeded random helper and setting up the builder with a feast table name and paint size before working through placement helpers for knives and other scattered items.

Writing build function...

Still writing SVG motifs...

Still adjusting cloth geometry and borders...

Drawing a triskelion-style triple-triangle emblem with a surrounding ring, layering a shadow copy and a dark-stroked outline for depth...

I'm also sketching the border lines and notches for the overall frame size, then moving on to map out rune glyph paths as SVG stroke coordinates...

Still writing rune glyphs...

Now I'm sketching the pot details—lathed iron body, stew contents, ladle, handle, and trivet—moving into the actual geometry code for each kitchen object.

Positioning the handle arc so its ends land on the rim, with small lug balls capping each end. For the ladle, I'm placing the bowl near the stew's edge and angling the rod outward so it rests over the rim, leaning toward the viewer's side of the table.

Now I'm defining a keg profile with coordinate pairs that shape its barrel silhouette, flat-headed ends tapering out to a wider middle radius.

I'm writing a paint function for the keg that alternates stave colors based on height and mixes in noise-based darkening for a weathered wood look, keeping the lathe coordinates as height and degree inputs.

Now I'm positioning the hoops as tori at interpolated radii based on the keg's barrel profile curve, with smaller hoops near the top and bottom heads, and setting segment counts for a reasonably smooth but low-poly look. I'm also placing circular decals on the keg heads using default face orientation.

I'm adding the tap assembly as a small cylinder with a lever box, and building the barrel cradle out of wood support boxes and diagonal chocks positioned along the barrel's resting points. Now I'm starting to place the bread loaf geometry on the board.

Still writing loaf placement...

I'll skip the braided loaf since the board's getting crowded, and just add a bread knife and flour dust for detail. Moving to cheese: placing a round wooden board with a cheese wheel on top, plus a cut wedge piece lying beside it for visual interest.

Repositioning the wheel further left to make room for the wedge so they don't overlap with the board edges, and sizing the wedge as a thin triangular slice resting against the wheel's cut face.

Trying a cylinder geometry with a reduced theta length to create a pie-slice cutout in the wheel, but realizing that leaves the cut side hollow without proper walls—so I'll keep the wedge as a separate piece placed in front instead. Also catching that the candelabra's base footprint now overlaps the cheese board's edge and needs repositioning.

I'm recalculating the x-axis footprints for the board, wheel, and wedge to avoid overlap with the candelabra base, shrinking the board's radius and shifting its center until the ranges clear each other by a reasonable margin.

Now I'm sizing the wedge to sit flush on top of the board matching the wheel's height, and planning to give it the same cheese color with surface holes and a knife detail stuck into it.
